basis: New mission, no workbook source. Researched via WebSearch (Sep 2026). Key facts: Taiwan relative poverty rate ~6.75-7.53% 2017-2023, 7.43% in 2022 (MOHW); low-income children (0-18) fell 117,012 (2016) to 90,245 (2021), near-poor children fell 135,819 (2016) to 107,010 (2021), together ~200,000 in 2021 (MOHW/CRC 兒少統計專區); Child Welfare League Foundation (兒福聯盟) survey: 20% of disadvantaged children have gone hungry at home and eaten snacks instead of a meal; ~20% rely on snacks when school lunch stops over long holidays; 11.0% of students skip breakfast 3+ days/week and arrive hungry; school lunch policy expanding city by city: Taipei free for all public+private elem/JHS since Sept 2025 (NT$87/NT$92 per meal); Kaohsiung free from 2026 school year (~NT$1.8B/yr, ~180,000 students); Tainan (~NT$56/meal) and Chiayi County (~NT$62/meal) free from 2026; Pingtung County free from 2026; Hsinchu City partial subsidy (NT$40/NT$45) with full waiver for disadvantaged (city government press releases, CNA, 風傳媒, 造咖); 2026 revision of 財政收支劃分法 ended central subsidy for domestic school-lunch ingredients, shifting cost to local budgets; Alliance of Taiwan Foodbanks (台灣食物銀行聯合會, ATF) — ~60 member food banks, ~300 partner NPOs, ~100 community refrigerators (84 fridges+16 freezers) nationwide, Taipei flagship store rescues ~20,000 kg food/yr for 200+ households/month, Hualien warehouse stores 500+ tonnes serving 20+ remote communities/schools (atf.tw); retail food waste — supermarkets/hypermarkets declared ~69,670 tonnes discarded Mar 2017-Jun 2023 (6 yrs), ~11,000 tonnes/yr, ~30 tonnes/day (foodnext.net/食力, government-mandated reporting). Level is carried by syntax and lexical load per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, not by word count.

slides.1: You've probably never actually seen a hungry classmate at your own school here, but here's a real question worth asking anyway. Would you know one if you did?
slides.2: SDG 2 also covers something we might genuinely call hidden hunger, which isn't about having zero food. It's about food that never arrives on time, or never arrives in enough amounts.
slides.3: Almost 200,000 children in Taiwan were counted as poor or near-poor most recently. Even so, the island seems to have plenty of food everywhere. A corner shop sits on nearly every block.
slides.4: Roughly one in five children living in poor households have gone without a proper meal at home. That comes from a countrywide study, and many turned to snack food instead that day.
slides.5: For plenty of these children, school lunch has become their single most reliable meal of the entire day. So once summer arrives, that dependable meal simply vanishes along with it.
slides.6: Almost one student in nine misses breakfast on more than half the school days, arriving to class already hungry. This sort of hunger looks like exhaustion, not obvious starvation.
slides.7: Real progress has finally started here. Since September 2025, Taipei has offered free lunch to every student there, now covering both younger and older kids this year too.
slides.8: Other municipalities have been following that lead as well. Kaohsiung's commitment alone runs to roughly 1.8 billion dollars a year, reaching about 180,000 pupils once things are fully rolled out.
slides.9: Beyond simply filling gaps, food banks now form a genuinely wider network across the island. The Alliance links roughly 60 separate food banks and almost 300 partner groups. It runs about 100 shared fridges too.
slides.10: Rather than following one uniform national rule, each city sets its own lunch subsidy. Prices range from about 40 dollars a meal up beyond 90 dollars elsewhere. It's a messy patchwork, though a fast-moving one.
slides.11: Food banks have expanded well beyond handing out dry canned goods lately. Taipei's main food bank alone rescues roughly 20,000 kilograms of food a year. That helps over 200 households every single month.
slides.12: However, if a community hasn't built that trust yet, good food can still end up wasted. It never actually reaches anyone in need. Turning near-expired bread into an actual meal still takes real effort.
slides.13: So here's the catch that rarely gets mentioned by anyone. Whether lunch is actually free still depends entirely on which school a child happens to attend that year.
slides.14: In 2026, a new funding law changed the picture a lot. Central government stopped paying for locally grown ingredients in school lunches, so each city must now cover that cost independently.
slides.15: Meanwhile, plenty of food still gets wasted regardless. Large retailers alone report discarding roughly 11,000 tonnes of food a year. Even so, food banks keep struggling to reach every family that needs them.
slides.16: So Taiwan genuinely has enough food, and more and more good policy too. What's still missing is one steady, equal system, rather than one depending on luck or location.
slides.17: Put another way, this was never really a story about Taiwan genuinely running short of food. Instead, it's a story about food consistently failing to reach every single child, day after day.
slides.18: This gap needs real tech fixes, things like smart routing apps and better delivery routes. That could very easily and genuinely describe someone whose studies already match this problem.
slides.19: The next community fridge or donation bin you happen to walk past is doing quiet work. It's covering a gap that official policy simply hasn't closed just yet.
slides.20: Whether a food bank stays stocked should never come down to chance. Building a system that reliably feeds every child, day after day, is the actual goal here.
